name: long_instruct
description: Long instruction-follow workload for steady-state TPS measurement under spec-decoding A/B. Designed to (a) amortize cold-start cost over a 600-token decode so the warm_step_rate dominates the result, (b) provide an instruction-follow prompt structured to favor EAGLE-3 drafter calibration via clear topical scope and predictable exposition style, (c) match the repo's existing spec-bench convention of greedy decoding + fixed seed so per-run RNG variance is eliminated and any cross-run delta reflects engine behavior not sampling chance. Pair with the base Instruct drafter (lmsys/SGLang-EAGLE3-Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507-SpecForge-Nex) for tightest drafter-target distribution match; the Coder variant (Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-SpecForge) will under-perform here because the workload is technical exposition not code. For sampled-temperature realism checks run long_instruct_sampled.json (T=0.4) alongside.

prompts.text:
Provide a comprehensive technical explanation of how a mixture-of-experts transformer model performs inference at decode time on consumer hardware. Structure your answer around five clearly labeled sections:

1. The router gating mechanism. Explain how the router computes gate logits from each token's hidden state, applies softmax to produce a distribution over experts, and selects the top-k experts via argsort. Note the typical values of k (2 for Mixtral, 8 for Qwen3, 8 for DeepSeek-V3) and the trade-off between routing sparsity and load balance.

2. The gather-FFN-scatter dispatch pattern. Walk through how the engine, having selected k experts per token, gathers the relevant hidden states for each expert, runs the gate-up-down FFN computation per expert, and scatters the weighted results back into the residual stream. Mention the gather and scatter as memory-traffic operations distinct from the FFN compute itself.

3. Why the bottleneck shifts from compute to memory bandwidth at batch size one. Explain that at decode time each token must read every activated expert's weights, that GEMV arithmetic intensity is roughly one FLOP per byte, and that this places decode firmly on the bandwidth-bound side of the roofline regardless of compute capacity.

4. How shared-expert architectures in DeepSeek-V2 and Qwen3.6 differ from pure routed-expert designs. Describe the shared expert as an always-active FFN that fires on every token and absorbs common-knowledge computation, allowing routed experts to specialize on the residual signal. Note the implication for quantization: the shared expert sees every token's error and therefore should be kept at higher precision than the routed experts.

5. Practical performance implications for consumer hardware. Explain what happens when the model is larger than available VRAM: experts must spill to system RAM and be paged in over PCIe at decode time. Mention the order-of-magnitude bandwidth drop from HBM to PCIe, the role of expert prefetching to hide that cost, and why hot-cold expert caching becomes the dominant performance optimization in this regime.

Be thorough but concise. Use short paragraphs and numbered points within each section where helpful.
